newsitem.title: UK: UK, Spain debate Gibraltar, without Gibraltarians.
newsitem.headline: UK, Spain debate Gibraltar, without Gibraltarians.

text.p: British Foreign Minister Malcolm Rifkind flies to Spain on Wednesday for talks on Gibraltar ready to warn that Britain will consider going to the European Court unless Spain agrees to recognise passports issued in the colony.
But the Gibraltar government, angered by the passport row, is refusing to take part.

The talks are the first since Peter Caruana was elected Gibraltar's new first minister last May pledging to improve strained links with both Britain and Spain, and since Jose Maria Aznar's Conservative government took power in Madrid last year.
But hopes that new political blood could help end years of wrangling over the colony at the tip of the Iberian peninsula and encourage more cooperation have been dashed.

Instead the talks are being overshadowed by a new row over passports. The Spanish government has signalled it is considering withdrawing recognition of the passports, issued to the people of the rocky outcrop by the British governor.
But Britain insists that it has every right to issue passports to citizens of its dependent territories and that Spain must recognise them under European Union laws.
A British official said the passports had been issued for years without problems and added: "We are absolutely clear that we have the legal right of the matter on our side on this."
The official said Britain was hoping Spain would drop its threat to withdraw recognition, but he added: "There will be no profitable discussion on Gibraltar if this is not resolved...
"If they (Spain) were to obstruct free movement, of course we would have to take it up with the (European) Commission and ultimately with the European Court."
Gibraltar is a constant irritant in relations between Britain and Spain, which claims sovereignty over the colony dominating the western entrance to the Mediterranean.
Gibraltarians say they do not want to become Spanish. But for Britain the colony's strategic importance has declined.

Britain would like to get Spain to set aside the sovereignty question to allow the negotiation of concrete cooperation deals, along the lines of British talks with Argentina on oil exploration around the Falklands.
But it is annoyed by what one official on Tuesday called Spain's "childish and irritating" habit of delaying people crossing the border between Spain and Gibraltar.
Caruana has continued tightening up laws to combat drugs trading and money laundering which was rife in the colony.

But despite a clampdown on the speedboats which ferried contraband between Africa and Europe, Spain has not responded, and last week delays at the border were up to two hours again, British officials said on Tuesday.
